name: Hawaiian religion
areas: the kapu system governs daily life among the eight islands
after the kapu is overthrown, family ʻaumākua, bones and sacred places remain; some practise the old faith as a co-religion
routes: Settlers from the Marquesas and greater Polynesia reach Hawaiʻi (by about 800)
Pāʻao, a priest or chief from Tahiti, brings the kapu (about 1200)
marks: Settled no later than 800 CE by people from the Marquesas and greater Polynesia, with a significant influx of Tahitians.

notes: Settlers from the Marquesas and greater Polynesia reach the Hawaiian Islands by about 800 and bring their religious beliefs; immigration continues to about 1300.
By tradition Pāʻao, a priest or chief from Tahiti, arrives around 1200 and the kapu system comes with him.
After Kamehameha the Great dies, Kaʻahumanu, Keōpūolani and the kahuna nui Hewahewa persuade Kamehameha II to overthrow the kapu system (1819).
Protestant missionaries arrive from the United States (1820); most aliʻi convert, and laws against ancient practices follow.
Max Freedom Long originates Huna, which scholars regard as a New Age mix and not traditional Hawaiian religion.
During the Hawaiian Renaissance of the 1970s the religion resurges; a suit over Kahoʻolawe (1976) forces the Navy to protect religious sites.
The unearthing of 1,000 graves on Maui (1988) leads to a hotel's relocation inland.
Protests begin over the Thirty Meter Telescope on Mauna Kea (2014), which some Hawaiians regard as their most sacred mountain.
src: Martha Warren Beckwith, The Kumulipo: A Hawaiian Creation Chant (University of Hawaii Press, 1981)
